Complete deletion-witness classificationI independently reconstructed the fundamental argument.Let  $G$  be bipartite,  $S$  a minimal forming set, and  $v\in S$  belong to a selected component with at least three vertices.Every vertex in such a component belongs to a selected three-vertex path. Consequently, after deleting  $v$ , the vertex  $v$  itself remains formed by the other two vertices of that path.Minimality therefore guarantees some previously omitted vertex  $x$  which becomes unformed after deleting  $v$ .There are precisely three possibilities.Case I:  $x$  is adjacent to  $v$ .Before deletion,  $x$  has at least one selected neighbour and is formed.After deletion, it cannot have two selected neighbours. If it has one remaining selected neighbour  $i$ , that neighbour must be inactive.Because  $i$  and  $v$  belong to the same bipartition class, deleting  $v$  cannot change the selected degree of  $i$ . Thus  $i$  was already isolated.The possibilities are exactly
$$N_S(x)=\{v\},$$
or
$$N_S(x)=\{v,i\},
\qquad d_S(i)=0.$$
Case II:  $x$  is not adjacent to  $v$ .Its selected neighbourhood does not change.Its failure to remain formed must therefore result from a selected neighbour  $u$  becoming inactive.There must have been exactly one selected neighbour, and  $u$ 's only selected partner must have been  $v$ :
$$N_S(x)=\{u\},\qquad N_S(u)=\{v\}.$$
These three possibilities exhaust the ways formation can fail.This is a genuine complete classification, not an argument that silently assumes induced stars.Direct-witness disjointnessCases I and II's first two possibilities are the direct witnesses.Each direct witness has exactly one active selected neighbour, its owner. Therefore a direct witness cannot serve two different active owners.A selected leaf in a component of order at least three necessarily has a direct witness: deleting the leaf leaves its centre active, so no other selected vertex can become inactive through that deletion.I find this argument correct.3.
